claims.text: Resistance of high-entropy alloys to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed primarily by a self-healing, mechanically robust oxide-passivation layer.
Increasing chromium concentration enables rapid re-passivation after mechanical disruption.
Rapid re-passivation maintains both corrosion protection and wear resistance.
Standard levels of passivating elements such as chromium promote typical oxide-film formation in the baseline alloy.
A moderate increase in chromium will promote formation of an improved oxide-passivation layer relative to the baseline.
The proposed mediator is a self-healing, high-hardness oxide-passivation film with enhanced surface stability.
Increasing chromium concentration produces a more uniform oxide layer.
Increasing chromium concentration produces a more adherent oxide layer.
The chromium-enhanced oxide layer better resists mechanical abrasion because of improved hardness and integrity.
The chromium-enhanced oxide layer better resists corrosive attack because of enhanced chemical stability.
The chromium-enhanced surface re-passivates rapidly when worn.
The oxide layer's combined mechanical and chemical functions mitigate synergistic wear-corrosion damage.
Under combined wear-corrosion testing, the chromium-enriched alloy will exhibit lower cumulative material loss than the baseline alloy.
The chromium-enriched alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion rate than the baseline alloy.
The chromium-enriched alloy will exhibit a lower wear-track depth than the baseline alloy.
The predicted benefit should hold when active oxide formation is viable during simultaneous mechanical and corrosive attack in an electrolyte.
The predicted benefit may fail in inert atmospheres that do not permit proper oxide formation.
The prediction may fail if increased chromium causes adverse phase formation under some processing regimes.
The baseline and chromium-modified alloys will be processed identically and tested under the same electrolyte, load, sliding speed, and temperature.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in combined material loss, or failure to observe improved oxide-layer stability or mechanical robustness, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
